title: The Value of School Facility Investments: Evidence from a Dynamic Regression Discontinuity Design
research_question: What is the causal effect of investments in public school facilities on local housing prices and student academic achievement? Do homebuyers value a marginal dollar of school facility spending at more than its cost, and does such spending translate into measurable gains in student test scores or changes in neighborhood composition?
data_description: The authors assemble a district-level panel covering California school districts from the late 1980s through 2006. School bond referendum data (year, bond amount, intended purpose, vote share, required threshold for passage, and turnout) come from the California Education Data Partnership and cover all general obligation bond measures sponsored by school districts between 1987 and 2006. Annual district-level fiscal variables (capital outlays, current instructional and non-instructional expenditures, long-term debt, state aid, total revenues) and enrollment/demographics are from the Common Core of Data (1995–2006). Annual average housing transaction prices, square footage, lot size, and sales volumes come from a proprietary Dataquick database covering all California housing transactions 1988–2005, aggregated from census block groups to school districts using GIS. Third- and fourth-grade math and reading test scores come from CLAS, Stanford-9, and CAT exams. Homebuyer income and race are from HMDA tract-level data (1992–2006).
institutional_context: California's school finance system is highly centralized following the 1971 Serrano v. Priest decision and 1978 Proposition 13, leaving districts with little discretion over current spending and producing per-pupil spending well below the national average, especially for capital. Proposition 46 (1984) allows districts to issue general obligation bonds for school construction, renovation, and maintenance, financed by local property tax increases for the duration of the bonds. Bond issues must be approved in local referenda, originally requiring a two-thirds supermajority and, beginning in 2001, a 55% threshold for proposals meeting certain accountability restrictions. Bond proceeds are legally restricted to pre-specified capital projects and cannot fund administrator salaries. Between 1987 and 2006, 629 of 1,035 districts voted on at least one bond, with many measures decided by narrow margins. Bonds account for roughly one-third of California school facility spending, with state aid being the main alternative source.
